title: How many lessons do I need to learn to sing?
blocks: How quickly a student progresses in singing lessons actually depends on several factors
How skilled is your teacher? Do they use effective methods, and can they pass their knowledge on to you clearly?

How well developed is your musical ear? If you have never sung before and find it hard to hear notes and repeat them, learning may take a little longer than for a student whose ear is already developed. The same goes for a sense of rhythm. But that doesn't have to be the rule if you follow your teacher's advice and practise persistently. Of course, new knowledge needs some time to settle. For complete beginners, developing the ear takes anywhere from three months to a year.

How much time do you have for practice? Next to factor number one, this is the most important factor. Once you have decided to take singing lessons, it is very important to be persistent and to set aside at least a little time every day for singing. On a day when you have no time at all, that can be just 10 to 15 minutes. Practising half an hour every day is recommended. The longest stretch without practice shouldn't exceed 24 hours. Of course, it won't be the end of the world if your commitments keep you from practising for a couple of days, but the more days you skip, the slower your singing will progress.
How often do you have lessons?

A student who has lessons once a week will progress more slowly than a student who has lessons two or three times a week. So if you have lessons less often than twice a week, you should check in more often with the teacher who follows your practice. Ideally, a student has lessons twice a week and, on the other days, the support of a teacher who makes sure the practice is heading in the right direction. My 24 Hours Singing Support offer includes daily support with your practice and a personal written practice guide tailored to your lessons alone.

So, if you have no trouble repeating a note you hear, you practise 30 minutes every day or every other day, and you use 24 Hours Online Singing Support once or twice a week, in two and a half to three months you should be happy with what you hear.

In the end, it all depends on your goals. We can't expect a complete beginner to become a professional after three months. In three months, a very hard-working beginner who practises constantly will be happy with what they hear and will come to love their voice, while knowing there is still more to work on. And a very hard-working student with previous musical experience who wants to perfect their singing can expect to be extremely pleased with the result and ready for new career successes.
I can guarantee this pace for my own work. If you have a different teacher, you should ask them this question, because in the end every teacher's pace is individual.

title: Proper everyday breathing as the key to a healthy life and good singing
blocks: You have surely heard the expression "to breathe with full lungs". It means living a fulfilled life, at full capacity. So what does natural, healthy breathing look like – breathing with full lungs, at their full capacity?

My dears, I will now explain how to begin learning to sing in a healthy way. We will start with the one thing you cannot sing without: breathing. The healthier the way you breathe, the more beautiful and natural your singing.
There is a difference between breathing while singing and the breathing we do every day.
In everyday breathing, the process goes like this:
In singing breathing, the process goes like this:
Here is the healthy way. Let's try to make it a habit.

Why through the nose? By its very anatomy, the nose is designed to filter out dust and impurities with the help of its tiny hairs, so cleaner air reaches the lungs. Its second function is to warm the air, so that it reaches the other respiratory organs warmer.
The belly fills with air and moves forward.
After the belly, the lower part of the lungs fills, the ribs expand, and then the upper part of the lungs fills. Important: the shoulders do not rise.
Exhale through the mouth or nose.
Exercises you can use for better everyday breathing:

Relax, straighten up, inhale through your nose and slowly exhale through your mouth. When you feel there is no more air, don't stop. There is still stale air left, which you will push out by drawing your belly straight back at an even pace (pulling it in) while saying "ha, ha, ha" in short bursts until you feel there is no more air in your lungs. You will also feel that your belly is pulled in completely.
This is one way of cleansing the body, because part of the air always stays in the lungs and remains unchanged.

The next exercise is to fill your lungs with air in the way described above (inhale through the nose, fill the belly with air so it moves straight forward, fill the lower part of the lungs as the ribs expand, fill the upper part of the lungs without raising the shoulders). Then hold your breath for 5 seconds.
This is followed by exhaling on the syllable "ha" for as long as there is air and until the belly is pulled in all the way.

Inhalations with essential oils (eucalyptus, rosemary, thyme) are recommended, as they cleanse the body of toxins and mucus. Besides detoxifying, they are also used to treat colds, flu and other respiratory illnesses.

Diet is very important for healthy lungs and for the health of the whole body in general. It is healthy to take in plenty of water, fruit and vegetables and to avoid sugar, flour, meat and dairy products.
Ginger root tea with lemon eases breathing and helps clear toxins and mucus from the airways. Also, eat a small piece of ginger with every meal.
For those who believe in affirmations, here are some meant for healthy lungs:
I have the ability to live a fulfilled life with full lungs. Whatever I imagine, I can also do. I love life completely.
ALWAYS be aware of your breathing. At first, while you are adopting this healthiest of habits. After that, proper breathing will become an everyday – yet priceless – activity.

title: Correct posture while singing
blocks: Every singer's posture should be natural so that all the muscles in the body are relaxed. When your everyday posture is correct, your posture while singing will also be natural and healthy, which guarantees a healthy, natural tone and a beautiful vibrato.
For a natural posture, look at yourself in the mirror and practise the following position until you have fully made it your own. This position applies to everyday standing, walking and sitting.
Ears, shoulders and hips are aligned – parallel, in one line.
The belly is slightly tightened, but we make sure our hips stay aligned with the shoulders and ears.
We always keep our elbows next to our hips.
The walk is soft, relaxed, balanced and rhythmic.
From this it follows that correct singing posture means:
When inhaling, the belly moves forward; when exhaling, it moves straight back at an even pace.
Both feet are slightly apart and planted firmly on the ground.
In this stance, the entire breathing apparatus and all the muscles should be relaxed.

The mouth is naturally open, the jaw drops in a relaxed way, as if we were saying the vowel "a" – but only as far as the jaw drops naturally (as when we say the English word "father"). We should keep the tongue as flat as we can, with its tip touching the roots of the lower front teeth; it doesn't curl upwards (again, as when you say the English word "father").

As we exhale, we imagine having a rubber ball in our mouth and think about it while singing. We imagine the breath dropping into the lower part of the lungs, and all the cavities being open, free and clear so the air flows unhindered into the belly and lungs. When we fully free the passage for the air and relax the throat, we get a beautiful, natural, well-shaped tone and a good vibrato.

From the very beginning, the air should leave through the mouth and not the nose, to avoid nasal singing. If someone sings and speaks nasally, this is successfully solved by changing the way they breathe.

title: What are the advantages of online lessons?
blocks: Online lessons have become part of our everyday lives and connect you with the best teachers around the world.
In person or online – there's no difference anymore!

Technology has advanced so far that there is absolutely no longer any question of whether one should learn online. Online lessons have become part of our everyday lives and connect you with the best teachers around the world.
Your teacher is always there! You get written instructions every day!

At any time of day you can send a recording of your singing, and you will hear back as soon as possible whether you are practising correctly. Your teacher can follow your progress continuously and give you feedback every day. In short – you have support 24 hours a day!

You can set the lesson schedule and the pace that suits you. You choose whether you want lessons twice or once a week, and you always get the time slot that fits your daily schedule best. You choose your favourite genres and favourite songs, and every lesson is a unique experience.

Finally – no more public transport or worrying about parking. You don't have to think about what to wear or whether you'll make it to class on time. You simply sit down in front of your computer or phone and start working on yourself.
You can have lessons wherever you happen to be, which makes this way of learning even more exciting! Not at home? No problem! All you need is an internet connection.
ONLINE lessons are MORE AFFORDABLE than private lessons held in person. This way of learning saves both time and money and brings fantastic results.
Without a doubt, thanks to internet technology
Fantastic experiences are within our reach today!

title: How to speak clearly, distinctly and beautifully?
blocks: If you speak clearly and distinctly, you leave a very good impression on the person you're talking to, and the idea you want to get across will be clear. That's why I advise you to set aside a little time to improve the way you speak.
The first thing to do is take a newspaper article, a book or anything else you can use to practise your reading.

Before you start reading, open your mouth as wide as you can and say each vowel – a, e, i, o, u – for a long time, stretching your mouth all the way. The air should go only forwards, as if there were a little ball in front of you that your breath has to turn.
Before you start reading, calm your thoughts. Calm down and take a deep breath. Make sure you have enough air in your lungs for the sentence that follows.
Start reading. How did the first sentence you read sound? Could it sound better? I believe it could.

Now read the same sentence again, but twice as slowly. You will probably feel the urge to speed up, because reading that slowly can be boring. :) But don't. Reading slowly has a purpose, so resist the feeling that you should speed up. If you rush, some word will surely remain unclear – and that shouldn't happen. Every word must be pronounced slowly enough to be clear.
Now read that sentence again and PRONOUNCE EVERY SYLLABLE (part) of each word CLEARLY. Say each syllable separately and slowly, and practise until every one is clear and distinct.
Gradually speed up and shorten the pauses between words until you manage to speak clearly at a normal pace.

When breathing and speaking, be sure to gently stop the airflow on tricky consonants such as s, z, r, t, ch, sh… When said quickly, these are the consonants that make a word unclear. That's why the difference between all the consonants, as well as between all the vowels, should be clear, and every single letter – every sound, vowel or consonant – deserves enough attention.
If you notice that you "flew over" any syllable, go back, slow down and say that syllable more slowly.

Practise whenever you're alone – in the car or walking down the street, while cleaning or ironing, or standing in front of the mirror. Always set aside a little time; it can be just a few seconds or minutes. What matters is that you think about it every day.
You can also slow down and pay attention to syllables when talking to other people. You'll see that you make remarkable progress if you seriously invest some time in your speaking skills.
It can be incredibly useful to give your words another second or two so they are pronounced completely correctly.

Deep breathing can help you slow down your speech, so give it special attention. Taking a deep breath before you speak will let you talk more slowly and have enough air for the whole phrase. You also need enough air because, when speaking, air leaves the mouth continuously and EVENLY.
If you speak more slowly, your voice will stay calm and you will sound clearer.
Pauses between sentences give you more time to think while speaking, so you can be more sure of what you're going to say.
Speak as if you were writing an essay or a letter: patiently, cheerfully and precisely.
Try to break your thoughts into logical, well-rounded parts. Always stay focused on the essence of what you want to say.
Expand your vocabulary. One right word can be much clearer than a flood of less precise ones.
Try to find the exact word you're looking for – and use it effectively.
Be careful not to use words incorrectly or in the wrong context; this could undermine the clarity of what you're trying to say, and you may not be understood the way you intended.
A word of caution: make sure the people you're talking to know the words you use with them.
Keep your audience in mind. Use simpler words if necessary.
Reading is a great way to expand your vocabulary. Read books, articles, essays; read things that interest or fascinate you.
Whenever you come across a word you don't know yet, look up what it means.
Try keeping a list of beautiful, useful, effective words. The more you use them in the right context, the more naturally they'll come to you – and your choice of words will get even better.

Think before you speak. Preparing what you're going to say reduces the risk of getting flustered and saying something you didn't plan. Even if you don't plan the exact words, take a moment to review your ideas, ask yourself what the essence of what you want to say is, and keep that idea in your head. Because the essence matters most of all.
Say the words quietly and slowly to yourself before you say them out loud. This can help you pronounce them correctly.
Speak with the right intonation. If you want to ask a question, your pitch should rise at the end of the sentence. Statements should end with confidence.
Pay attention to which syllables are stressed in a sentence.
And finally, emphasise all the words that carry the essence of the sentence.

title: Why is singing healthy?
blocks: Singing boosts self-confidence: when we discover our passion and start pursuing it, we become aware of our own qualities.
In singing lessons we adopt the healthiest way of breathing and holding our body. The way we breathe while singing helps lower stress hormones, creates a feeling of calm and lowers blood pressure.
Singing requires focus and constant concentration; it greatly contributes to a clear mind and improves cognitive abilities.
Singing improves diction and supports the development of the speech apparatus.
By singing correctly we discover the natural beauty of our voice, which is especially valuable for the proper functioning of the thyroid gland.

title: What if I don't like the colour of my voice?
blocks: It has happened to all of us: we perceive our speaking voice one way, and then, when we hear how we sound on a recording, in most cases we are more or less disappointed. What is actually going on?

When we speak, we hear our own voice as sound carried internally, through the bones. The result is low frequencies that don't reach us through the air. When we record our voice, we hear it without those low frequencies, because it reaches us from the outside. It then sounds higher and different – not the way we expected. Most people are disappointed at that point. However, there really is no need to be.
We need to know that this is the voice we were given, one we should learn to love and accept – but, above all, one we need to get used to.
Today's technology helps with that, because it lets us record our voice and listen back many times.

What we are advised to do – and it takes only a little willpower – is, as already mentioned, record our own voice on a recording device and then ask ourselves a few questions: How does my voice sound to me? What are the truly beautiful qualities of my voice? What makes it less beautiful, and what should I change? What beautiful feelings can my voice awaken in the listener?
We need to understand what its essence really is and where its beauty lies.

It is best to record your voice several times, listen back again and again and ask yourself the questions above. The more often we hear our voice and the more we think about it and what makes it beautiful, the faster we will accept it. This is our vocal colour, which will stay with us all our lives, so we need to focus above all on its good sides. All the good sides we focus on and work on will very soon come to the fore.

Whatever we notice that doesn't sound beautiful enough, we should try to correct. If our voice is quiet, we can try to speak louder, while gaining control over our voice so it doesn't turn into shouting. If we speak too loudly, we will try to speak more quietly – but not too quietly – so that the volume is pleasant. If it seems we speak too high (so-called "screeching"), we will first try to control the pitch of our voice (trying to speak a little lower, deeper). If we speak nasally, we will make sure that while speaking the air passes mainly through the mouth, that we speak "on the breath" and don't use the nose (only to inhale).

When it comes to singing and vocal colour, it's a similar story. Recording, listening back and analysing the voice by asking the questions above are the first steps. Beyond that, we need to work on correct singing technique, healthy posture, breathing, intonation stability and so on.

What I can guarantee you as a teacher is that each of us has a unique vocal colour, that every vocal colour has enough beautiful sides waiting to be discovered, and that anything in the voice that sounds less beautiful can be changed by paying attention to correct breathing, correct pronunciation of vowels and consonants, and the way we express ourselves.

title: Correct breathing while singing
blocks: Air is our fuel. Air is everything. Air is a singer's power. Without air there is no singing

As we said in the section "Everyday breathing as the key to a healthy life and beautiful singing", singing breathing differs from everyday breathing only in that the rest comes between the inhale and the exhale.

So, in everyday breathing, we inhale, exhale and rest for a moment. Then start over. If you haven't read the section "Everyday breathing as the key to a healthy life and beautiful singing", you'll find there everything you should adopt BEFORE you start learning correct singing breathing.

In singing breathing, we inhale, REST, and then exhale. What kind of rest are we talking about? This rest is the short pause after the inhale and before we release the voice. Once we release the voice, the exhale follows – as even and as slow as possible.
Singing will only be good if we control our breathing and our voice.

What connects everyday and singing breathing (if everyday breathing is correct, singing breathing will be correct too) is the INHALE and EXHALE, which happen in the same way. What do they look like? The same as in everyday breathing:
We fill the belly with air (the belly must move forward so that as much air as possible fits in).
We fill the lower part of the lungs and the ribs expand
We fill the upper part of the lungs without raising the shoulders (!)
The belly moves back, slowly and evenly.
The throat is as relaxed as possible.
This breathing should be practised every day until it becomes a complete habit. This way of breathing should become the most important part of our singing technique.

title: How to overcome the fear of performing in public?
blocks: Performing in public can be a stressful experience if we have negative expectations in our head and fear what the people in the audience will think. There are ways to help you finally relax and gain more confidence on stage.

Give yourself enough time to prepare absolutely every detail of the upcoming performance. And make sure that some time before – a day or two before the performance – you are already ready and still have enough time for anything unforeseen. Give yourself enough time to learn everything you will present. Give what you need to present enough time to settle, so that all that information is familiar, well established and close to you. What you present must never be a bogeyman for you. If it's a performance, what you perform should be fully absorbed, thoroughly familiar – a part of you. If you sing, work on those songs over a longer period, practise enough, explore what else could be improved, and seek professional support.
Give yourself time for creativity, to immerse yourself in what you are presenting and to become one with it. Because it's your story you're telling, and it's the reason you're there.
Try to anticipate as many situations as possible that could come up unexpectedly, and prepare for them too. The more organised you are, the less nervous you'll be.

Whenever you feel fear right before the performance, breathe in deeply and slowly while counting to 4, then hold your breath while counting to 3, and slowly and evenly breathe out while counting to 5. When we are afraid, our breath stops and we tense up – and if we hold our breath, we hold on to the tension too.

Repeat this exercise until you feel calm. Here too, time plays the main role: if you start preparing earlier, you have time to use your breathing to positively influence the anxiety that comes up when you think about the upcoming performance.

The moment you experience a negative thought, you gain the power to steer it. You have two options: accept it, believe it and let it steer you – or accept it so that you can steer it. It can come, but it mustn't upset your plans. Simply think about what you can control and what depends on you, and work on that at every possible moment. If you have worked with dedication and given it your all, success will come. Things you can't control are in the minority anyway; there's no point in thinking about them.

Think about and write down the exact goals of this performance – what you would like to achieve and what impression you want to leave. How exactly would you like your performance to look? What is the most basic thing you want to achieve, without which this performance wouldn't be a success? Write it all down, and then take care of every single detail needed to reach your goals. Don't forget that all these details require the preparation time we talked about at the beginning.
5. What doesn't kill us makes us stronger

Keep in mind the whole time that the situation ahead cannot kill us, and it will pass. Don't forget that, however important the event, afterwards everything will be relatively the same: this situation is not an ending, not a finish line – life goes on. After the performance we'll have the chance to correct whatever needs correcting, to progress and to become even better at what we do.

Only experience will make your performance flawless. Don't judge yourself harshly, but work on making your current presentation as good as possible. If you work enough for the performance, you will surely be satisfied. When you have truly given your best, leave the rest of the space to experience and time to fill in any remaining gaps, if there are any.

The more experience we have, the smaller the stage fright. But if you give yourself enough time, these tips will help you succeed at every performance. Make an effort to build your self-confidence solely through persistent work on yourself – because there simply is no other trick – and don't let unjustified fears spoil what you are fighting for.
